title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) to measure whether embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loop increases detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated network configurations and improves bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (N=270 tasks), gpt-5-mini as generator, and a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet deterministic emulator/verifier as ground truth, the verifier accepted the single generated candidate for every paired task: baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify→optional bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%); repairs were not invoked. The paired difference is 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI [0.00,0.00], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). This outcome is a provenance‑anchored null that results from two preregistered design facts recorded in the execution manifest: (A) a shared_initial_candidate sampling semantics (execution_contract.independent_condition_generation = false) caused one generated candidate per task to be evaluated under both arms, and (B) the chosen generator/prompt produced verifier‑acceptable outputs for the synthetic suite. We release the full preregistration, execution traces, validator traces, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifest so the community can deterministically reproduce the run and run minimal follow‑ups that change only the sampling semantics (e.g., set independent_condition_generation=true and permit independent generation per arm).

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed as intent‑to‑configuration translators in NetOps (intent‑based networking). Their stochastic generation, however, may produce syntactically plausible but operationally unsafe device commands. A common safety architecture is Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR): (1) generate candidate configuration(s); (2) deterministically verify via a formal or black‑box oracle; (3) when rejected, provide diagnostics to a bounded repair loop that attempts to produce a verifier‑accepted candidate. The goal of this preregistered study (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) was confirmatory: quantify the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic verifier into an LLM pipeline on the probability that generated outputs are detected/rejected and on bounded repair success. We emphasize up front a critical methodological point raised by the execution: the sampling semantics used in a preregistered design determine whether the original estimand (marginal verifier effect under independent sampling per arm) is testable. In the run reported here the execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=false; see execution/execution_manifest.json), producing a single generated candidate per task that both arms evaluated. That design choice is artifact‑anchored (see Disclosure) and is the proximate cause of the degenerate contingency observed. We document the run, the provenance of every primary number, the preregistered analysis, and provide a minimal deterministic recipe (artifact‑anchored) for a controlled follow‑up that validly tests the original estimand.
sections.related_work: Prior work motivates the GVR pattern and verifier anchoring across domains where determinism or compliance is required (generate‑but‑verify in code and regulated domains; Convergent Correctness and related proposals; see doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899). Formal network verification frameworks (NetKAT/Weighted NetKAT and related decision procedures) provide natural deterministic oracles for NetOps pipelines and have been proposed as verifiers for generated configs (see doi:10.1145/3808318). Recent systems work integrates LLMs, RAG and verifier checks in intent pipelines; these provide architectures and pilot studies but typically lack preregistration, deterministic hash manifests, or full emulator‑anchored validation. Our study differs by preregistering a paired estimand, freezing the experiment, executing the run with comprehensive deterministic logging (per‑artifact SHA‑256s), and releasing verifier traces for every episode so readers can inspect exactly what was generated, validated, and scored.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan. The preregistration (netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) was frozen before execution; archived preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (within‑task difference in proportion of verifier acceptances/rejections). Design choices (preregistered): paired within‑task evaluation with Npairs = 270 (SyntheticNetOpsIntentConfig_v1: 3 vendor syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks). Sampling semantics executed: shared_initial_candidate (execution_contract.independent_condition_generation = false) — a single LLM generation per task was evaluated in both baseline and guarded conditions (this is recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json). Planned model budget and calls: planned_episode_count = 540; maximum_model_calls = 540; observed model_calls_used = 270 (one shared generation per pair). Generator and verifier. Declared generator: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) via provider openai_responses. Deterministic verifier/emulator: Dockerized Kathará/Mininet deterministic environment used as ground truth; we recorded complete validator traces per episode (execution/scoring/*.json). Repair policy. Guarded arm: verifier invoked; if the verifier rejected a candidate, a bounded LLM‑guided repair loop (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1 as preregistered) would be invoked. The run recorded repair invocations and traces; in this execution repairs were never invoked because no initial candidate was rejected. Metrics and statistical plan. Primary test: paired binary comparison using exact McNemar two‑sided test; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power/MDE. The preregistered power calculation assumed independent per‑arm stochastic sampling (independent_condition_generation = true). Because the executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics, the preregistered MDE/power assumptions do not apply to the observed contingency; we make this explicit and artifact‑traceable in Results and Discussion. Reproducibility and deterministic logging. We archived raw model responses, scoring JSONs, provider call traces, and a full per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifest (see execution/*). Representative artifact hashes cited throughout: execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b07e1ffabb163657f56ae893fd65fc12d5307ea1ff3bb98f7cf43329a; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 62cd99d7bf35cab7ee751f4faae9004784597d06684b884750e66083a3e52f21. Missingness, retries and exclusions. Model/API call failures: preregistered retry policy allowed up to two retries per failed call; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0 in the execution manifest. Exclusion rules: only exclude tasks when emulator failures prevent ground truth; no exclusions occurred.
sections.results: Execution and primary counts (artifact‑anchored). Planned episodes: 540 (270 paired tasks). Completed: 540; failed: 0. Model calls used: 270 (one shared generation per pair as preregistered). Baseline accepted (validator decision): 270/270 = 100%. Guarded final acceptances: 270/270 = 100%. Discordant pairs: n10 = 0 (guarded accepted, baseline rejected), n01 = 0 (baseline accepted, guarded rejected); n11 = 270, n00 = 0. Repairs invoked in guarded arm: 0. Primary inference. Observed paired difference = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000; bootstrap_seed = 1729). Diagnostic interpretation. The degenerate CI and p value arise arithmetically from zero discordant pairs (n10=n01=0) under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics; these inferential quantities therefore do not provide evidence that a verifier is useless in general. Instead they quantify a conditional result: given the single generated candidate per task (the same candidate evaluated in both arms) and given the chosen generator/prompt settings (gpt-5-mini, model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...), every candidate was verifier‑acceptable for the synthetic task bank. Verifier↔emulator concordance. For the reserved validation subset (54 tasks) the verifier↔emulator agreement was 54/54 (no false_accepts or false_rejects) as recorded in the per‑episode scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json). Representative episode artifacts. Example scoring and validator traces are available for inspection: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256 350bfaa2eec0deb0e16121f5e7effa2d8743d28f3f014856107acfabbb42d87e) contains the normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, touched_field_count, and the validator decision. The full per‑artifact manifest and raw transcripts are archived under execution/* (SHA‑256s cited above).
sections.discussion: Why this provenance‑anchored null occurred. Two preregistered, artifact‑recorded design facts jointly produced the observed contingency: (1) the execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (execution_contract.independent_condition_generation = false) so a single generated candidate per task was evaluated in both arms; (2) with the frozen prompt and model settings as archived (gpt-5-mini; execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...), the generator produced verifier‑acceptable candidates for the entire synthetic suite. Both facts are recorded and reproducible (execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/raw_results.jsonl). Methodological lesson. Sampling semantics are an essential part of the estimand: a paired test that aims to measure the marginal effect of inserting a verifier requires independent stochastic generation per arm (independent_condition_generation = true) or multiple independent draws per arm. Under shared candidate evaluation the verifier cannot change the observed accept/reject outcome unless the verifier is non‑deterministic or the repair loop is invoked on one arm only; consequently, using shared candidates converts the estimand into a conditional quantity (marginal effect given identical candidate). Practical operational implication. A verifier is still operationally useful—e.g., as an on‑line gate, human‑in‑the‑loop checkpoint, or regulator—but a careful experimental design (independent per‑arm generation or multiple draws) is required to measure its marginal effect under stochastic generators. Minimal deterministic reproducible follow‑up recipe (artifact‑anchored). To produce a run that validly tests the original preregistered estimand, change only the following fields in the archived execution JSONs and re‑run the provided harness: (A) set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation = true so each arm receives an independent generation; (B) ensure model call budget permits one generation per arm per task (set maximum_model_calls >= 540 and/or planned_episode_count = 540 accordingly); (C) set a non‑zero temperature or provide per‑generation seeds in execution/model_configuration.json to expose stochastic variation (the execution artifact contains the field names to edit); (D) optionally increase maximum_repair_calls_per_task to >1 to test bounded repair convergence. All these field names and the exact artifact locations are present in the provided preregistration and execution manifest (preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbad..., execution_manifest path recorded). Limitations and threats to validity. Synthetic tasks and emulator vs production gaps limit external validity; single‑model evaluation limits generality; verifier rule‑set sensitivity and bounded repair budget restrict construct coverage; importantly, the executed sampling semantics altered the estimand/power balance and make the run conditional rather than a direct test of the originally preregistered marginal estimand. We enumerate these limitations and provide full artifact pointers so readers can deterministically run the follow‑up variant that restores independent sampling.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired experiment integrating a deterministic network verifier into an LLM GVR pipeline and published the complete execution, scoring, and analysis bundle. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics (one generated candidate per task evaluated in both arms) and the chosen generator settings (gpt-5-mini), every candidate in the synthetic suite was verifier‑acceptable and no repairs were invoked, producing an artifact‑verifiable paired difference of 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.0). The central methodological conclusion is that generation sampling semantics are decisive: measuring a verifier's marginal effect requires independent per‑arm sampling (or multiple independent draws) and an execution budget that permits it. We release the preregistration (SHA‑256 8ae7fbad...), the master prompt reference (provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e...), the execution manifest and raw results (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b...), and complete scoring traces so others can reproduce the run, inspect every validator trace, and run the minimal follow‑up that changes only the independent_condition_generation field to test the original estimand. All run artifacts and exact SHA‑256 manifests are archived under execution/* and analysis/* for deterministic verification and targeted follow‑up experiments.

limitations: Synthetic task suite and emulator limitations: the task bank (SyntheticNetOpsIntentConfig_v1) and Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator approximate operational patterns (shutdown→change→restore, make‑before‑break), but do not fully capture production vendor heterogeneity, hardware failures, or multi‑vendor interactions.
Single‑model evaluation: only gpt-5-mini (model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...) was used; results do not generalize across generators without further runs.

Sampling semantics versus preregistered power: the preregistered power/MDE calculations assumed independent per‑arm sampling (independent_condition_generation=true). The executed shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per pair and therefore changed the estimand; the original MDE/power assumptions are inapplicable to the observed contingency.

Bounded repair budget and policy sensitivity: the guarded arm used a bounded repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1); multi‑attempt repairs or different repair prompting strategies could change practical repair success rates.

Verifier rule‑set sensitivity: we used a single deterministic verifier rule set (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and the observed verifier↔emulator agreement was perfect on the reserved validation subset; more permissive or conservative rule sets would alter false_accept/false_reject tradeoffs.

Emulator vs production gap: validator acceptance in the emulator does not guarantee identical behavior on vendor devices or in complex production control planes; further testbed/field validation is required before operational deployment.
